newsitem.title: USA: Dollar rises after giant Japan trade surplus. [CORRECTED 21:30 GMT]
newsitem.headline: Dollar rises after giant Japan trade surplus. [CORRECTED 21:30 GMT]

text.p: The dollar rose Wednesday, overcoming early selling against the yen sparked by news of a sharp gain in Japan's trade surplus in May, which included a surge in its surplus with the United States.

Buying to cover short-selling also lifted the dollar against the German mark amid signs that European Economic and Moneteary Union is moving forward despite big questions about key nations cutting their budget deficits enough to ensure a strong start to the euro currency.
The dollar recovered after dipping under 113 yen when Japan reported that its trade surplus swelled 222 percent to 738 billion yen ($6.53 billion), in May from a year earlier.

Traders -- whose fears that the weak yen would pump up Japan's exports were borne out -- had sold dollars this week, expecting a big jump. The surplus was at the very upper end of expectations, but traders used the quick decline to take profits before data on the U.S. trade deficit on Thursday.

Japan's surplus with the United States rose 93 percent. The report came one day before the U.S. Commerce Department was to release its international trade figures, which are expected confirm a deterioration in the U.S. trade position.

"People were genuinely interested to sell," said Jeffrey Yu, a senior dealer at Sanwa Bank Ltd. "But maybe people realised we still have Thursday's U.S. trade number and that is expected to reconfirm the (Japan) trade surplus is huge."

Few expect the Japanese trade surplus (corrects from deficit) to be the primary topic of discussion at the weekend summit meeting of Group of Seven big industrial nations -- Britain, France, Germany, Italy, Japan, Canada and the United States -- in Denver.
But trade issues are expected to come up in one-on-one talks between Japanese Prime Minister Ryutaro Hashimoto and U.S. President Bill Clinton in Denver.
"Nobody expects anything special to come out of it regarding foreign exchange, but one always has to be cautious," Yu said.
The dollar ended at 113.65 yen, up from 113.32 yen at Tuesday's close. It also sprang back from an overnight low of 1.7225 marks, ending at 1.7333 marks, up from 1.7305 Tuesday.

"The tug and pull (on the dollar vs. marks) remains based on whatever you believe the appropriate EMU scenario is going to be," said Rick Gomes, managing director at Republic National Bank of New York.

On Wednesday, the Financial Times newspaper reported that the French deficit is set to exceed by at least half a percent the requirement that states wishing to qualify for the single currency must have deficits not larger than 3.0 percent of gross domestic product.

Also, Belgium said it would sell gold reserves in the form of commemorative coins to reduce the country's debt, which boosted the dollar on fears that one-time budget measures mean the mark would be supplanted with a weak euro.
In other trading, the dollar rose to 1.4470 Swiss francs from 1.4447 and to Canadian $1.3935 from C$1.3865.
